projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: Before I left London for a holiday here I had a talk with P who had been away. He jibbed a little but would consider your idea for a publisher here if there are not any printer’s errors. I asked to write you. I sent you in a previous letter my own suggestion. Anyhow I gave him the list of the committee I proposed when you agree about the joint scheme and I asked Pinker to place my share at his disposal already.
Did you see what the Frankfurter published under my name? A thing I never wrote a word of and they will not even apologise.
This is a nice old town but the devil’s own weather.

note.p: JJ wrote this letter on a “Lettercard” of the Lord Warden Hotel in Dover, England, where “the proprietors were Irish and friendly” (Ellmann, JJ 641). JJ had gone to Dover with Nora and Lucia for a holiday before returning to Paris from their stay in England (see JJ to Pound, 21 July 1931, notes). In part, the Dover trip was made to keep track of Lucia, who had decided to cross over to France to join Giorgio and his wife, Helen Kastor Fleischman Joyce (1894-1963). The manager of the Lord Warden, named McGee, offered to accompany Lucia across the Channel and see her through Customs, and JJ rewarded McGee’s daughter, Joan, with a signed copy of his Pomes Penyeach (Gordon Bowker, James Joyce: A New Biography [New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2011], 423-24).

The non-message side of this lettercard shows two photo-chromolithographic images: one of the hotel and the other of a beach and bathers, captioned “View of Dover Castle and Cliffs from the Hotel.” The Lord Warden Hotel (named for an official title of the Duke of Wellington) was designed for luxury and splendor, and hosted many famous figures during its history, including Charles Dickens and George Eliot. In 1924, Frederick Hotels Ltd. acquired the lease and refurbished the hotel in grand contemporary style. In 1927, the hotel had 110 rooms beginning at 8s. 6d. Breakfast started at 2s. 6d.; lunch, 5s.; and dinner, 7s. 6d. (Karl Baedeker, Great Britain: Handbook for Travellers, 8th rev. ed. [Leipzig: Karl Baedeker, 1927], 14). The lettercard images were produced by Photochrom Co. Ltd., London and Tunbridge Wells, England, a company that was established in 1896 and held the exclusive English license for the Swiss photochrom process, which the firm used to produce a great number of view-cards of England and Europe (http://www.metropostcard.com/publishersp1.html).

div.note: JJ was attempting to help Pound find a British publisher for his collected prose writings (not his Cantos, as Ellmann erroneously reports [LIII 217 n.4]), and had been consulting Laurence Edward Pollinger (1898-1976), who was then with the London-based literary agency, Curtis Brown. This plan for British publication did not materialize. For a fuller account, see JJ to Pound, 21 July 1931, notes.

As part of his effort to find a British publisher for Pound’s collected prose, JJ was attempting to raise funds for the venture through a committee of subscribers, partly because, as JJ noted, “the book is so long (E.P. says it is 1½ Ulysses) and times are so bad” (LIII 217). In addition to himself, JJ sought subscriptions from the American writer and publisher Robert McAlmon (1895-1956), the American poet and lawyer Archibald MacLeish (1892-1982), and the Rumanian sculptor Constantin Brancusi (1876-1957) (LIII 217) (see also JJ to Pound, 21 July 1931, notes).

note.p: James B. Pinker and Sons, a London literary agency. The British literary agent James Brand Pinker (prob. 1862 or 1863-1922) had acted for JJ until his death, having “little luck in marketing [JJ’s] peculiar merchandise” but serving as “the amiable recipient of the innumerable letters about small matters which Joyce soon began painstakingly to send him” (Ellmann, JJ 384). Pinker represented numerous modernist authors, including Henry James, Joseph Conrad, Ford Madox Ford, T.S. Eliot, D.H. Lawrence, Katherine Mansfield, and Dorothy Richardson (for additional details, see JJ to Pound, 3 April 1915, notes).

After Pinker’s death, his sons Eric Seabrooke (1891-1973) and James Ralph (1900-1959) continued to assist JJ with translation rights, “Work in Progress,” the piracies of Samuel Roth, and other matters. (There were two sons, not three, as Ellmann mistakenly suggests [LIII 65 n.10].) But the firm, James B. Pinker and Sons, struggled financially. Eric left for the United States in 1930, continued to work as a literary agent in New York City, pleaded guilty in 1939 to charges of grand larceny involving his work for clients, and was sentenced to a prison term of two-and-one-half to five years. Ralph carried on his father’s firm in London, but JJ complained that he was given to “bungling things in firstrate fashion” (LIII 236). Ralph was declared bankrupt in 1941, and just over a year later he was convicted of fraud and sentenced to a year’s imprisonment (J.H. Stape, “‘The Pinker of Agents’: A Family History of James Brand Pinker,” The Conradian, vol. 34, no. 1 [Spring 2009]: 111-43).

In July 1931, the Frankfurter Zeitung published a short story entitled “Vielleicht ein Traum,” misattributing it to “James Joyce” as author. The mistake was an innocent one. The German translator, Irene Kafka (1888-1942), or her secretary, had accidentally substituted JJ’s name for that of an English writer, Michael Joyce (b. 1903), who had originally published the story, “Perchance to Dream,” in The London Mercury, vol. 23, no. 124 (December 1930): 110-17. It is a strange mood piece, laced with crime, violence, and nightmare. JJ may have thought that the opening phrase was intended to exploit an association with Leopold Bloom: “It seemed to him that he was a commercial traveller.” JJ was certain the misattribution was “a forgery and a defamation,” and he told Sylvia Beach on 13 August 1931 that he had “sent off 36 letters and 11 wires on the F.Z. affair” (James Joyce’s Letters to Sylvia Beach, 1921-1940, ed. Melissa Banta and Oscar A. Silverman [Bloomington: Indiana University Press, 1987], 174, 175).

The Frankfurter Zeitung printed an explanation, and Irene Kafka and Michael Joyce offered regrets, but nothing would placate JJ, who continued his letter campaign over the perceived outrage, hired counsel, and was preparing for battle with a second Samuel Roth. JJ’s German and English lawyers sensibly suggested that a lawsuit would be pointless: any trifling damages would be swallowed up in legal fees, and public opinion would deem JJ’s attitude “vindictive and exacting and unworthy of a writer of standing and repute – infra dig” (Ellmann, JJ 639-40; LIII 226-31). JJ reluctantly dropped the matter and, according to Ellmann, paid the legal fees – more than he did for the lawyers who had represented him in the Roth litigation of 1927-1929 (see JJ to Pound, 28 March 1928, notes). Michael Joyce went on to write works of fiction, history, and biography, including Peregrine Pieram (1936), Ordeal at Lucknow (1938), My Friend H (1948), Edinburgh: The Golden Age (1951), and Edward Gibbon (1953).

div.note: It. standard phrase for concluding a letter, “kind regards.”
